summary: Describes a way to resynchronize the OSPF link state database out of band, without tearing down adjacency, so a router can catch up without disrupting routing. This memo is informational.

eli5.summary: Routers keep a shared map. If one router's map gets out of date, this lets it quietly fetch a fresh copy on the side without making everyone redo their work.

questions: resync ospf database without adjacency reset
what is ospf out-of-band lsdb resynchronization
what is the ospf r-bit in dbd packets
how does ospf resync without resetting adjacency
subtitle: How two OSPF routers can re-sync their link state databases without dropping the adjacency between them.

tldr.problem: The OSPF standard cannot resynchronize two routers' link state databases without pushing the neighbor state machine back to ExStart, which removes the adjacency from the router-LSAs and can cause routing table flaps.
tldr.mechanism: Capable routers advertise an LR-bit in Link-Local Signaling data, then run the usual database exchange with an R-bit set in every Database Description packet, while an OOBResync flag makes the rest of the router keep treating the neighbor as fully adjacent.
tldr.outcome: The memo records a vendor-specific mechanism that predates Graceful OSPF Restart and is not an IETF standard. It was later updated by RFC 9454.

today: RFC 4811 is an Informational memo describing a vendor-specific mechanism, not an IETF standard, and it was updated by RFC 9454. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Resynchronization Problem
sections.content:
In OSPF, two routers that have reached the Full state announce their adjacency in their router-LSAs. Asynchronous flooding keeps their link state databases (LSDBs) in step as the topology changes.

If the routers need to resynchronize for some other reason, the OSPF standard (RFC 2328) forces the neighbor state machine into ExStart. That removes the adjacency from the router-LSAs, which may be unacceptable if the goal is to avoid routing table flaps during resynchronization.

RFC 4811 provides out-of-band (OOB) LSDB resynchronization to avoid this. The abstract says it is a vendor-specific mechanism, proposed before Graceful OSPF Restart (RFC 3623), implemented by at least one major vendor and deployed in the field; the document exists to capture the details for public use. It is not an IETF standard.
sections.eli5: Normally, fixing an out-of-date map means the two routers pretend they have stopped working together for a while, and that upsets everyone else. This memo is a way to fix the map without that fuss.

sections.title: The Approach in Brief
sections.content:
The solution changes three things. The Database Description (DBD) packet gets a new R-bit that marks out-of-band resynchronization, and every DBD packet sent during the procedure has it set. The neighbor data structure gets two new fields: one for the neighbor's OOB capability and one saying that resynchronization is in progress. And a new bit in the Extended Options (EO) TLV, defined by RFC 4813, lets a router announce that it supports the technique.

The in-progress field means implementations can keep using their existing neighbor state machine code. The RFC stresses that the operation of the neighbor state machine itself is not changed.
sections.eli5: Three small additions are needed: a sticker on the messages saying "this is a quiet resync", a note in each router's address book, and a way to say "I know how to do this".

sections.title: The LR-Bit and the OOBResync Flag
sections.content:
The LR-bit (LSDB Resynchronization) is a new bit in the Link-Local Signaling (LLS) Extended Options TLV, with value 0x00000001. Routers that support the technique set it in the LLS block attached to both Hello and DBD packets. No bit is set in the standard OSPF Options field, in packets or in LSAs.

The neighbor data structure gets a flag called OOBResync, meaning the router is currently doing OOB resynchronization with that neighbor. It is set when the router initiates the procedure. It is cleared when the neighbor structure is first created, when the neighbor state machine drops below ExStart, when it moves to ExStart because a DBD packet with the R-bit clear arrived, and when it reaches Full. The flag can be true only in the ExStart, Exchange or Loading states.
sections.eli5: The LR-bit is a badge saying "I can do quiet resyncs". The OOBResync flag is a sticky note that says "we are in the middle of one with this neighbor" and gets thrown away when it is over or goes wrong.

sections.title: How DBD Packets Are Handled
sections.content:
DBD packets carry a new R-bit next to the I, M and MS flags. A router sets it when the OOBResync flag is true for that neighbor. Routers that support the technique should always set the LR-bit in Hello and DBD packets, so the stored Options of the initial DBD packet later show whether a neighbor is capable.

Incoming DBD processing changes in three steps:

  1. If the OOBResync flag is set and the packet has no R-bit, ignore the packet and generate a SeqNumberMismatch event.
  2. If the flag is clear and the packet has the R-bit set: when the neighbor is in Full and the I, M and MS bits are all set, set the flag, move to ExStart and process the packet as in RFC 2328. Otherwise ignore the packet, and also generate SeqNumberMismatch if the state is Exchange or higher.
  3. Otherwise, process it as RFC 2328 says.

A DBD packet with the R-bit set from a sender known to be OOB-incapable is dropped and also raises SeqNumberMismatch. If the receiver is chosen as Master, it may speed things up by replying immediately to the first OOB DBD packet.

Time in ExStart, Exchange and Loading with the flag set must be limited, for example by capping retransmissions. If the adjacency does not reach Full in time, the requester may stop trying over that adjacency, perhaps resynchronizing through another neighbor on the segment, or fall back to the legacy method by clearing the flag and leaving the state machine in ExStart. The neighbor may cancel the OOB procedure.
sections.eli5: Each message in the quiet resync carries the sticker. If a message shows up without it, or at a strange moment, the router ignores it. If things drag on for too long, the router gives up and does it the old, noisy way.

sections.title: Starting It and Keeping the Adjacency Visible
sections.content:
To start, a router first checks the LR-bit in the Options stored in the neighbor structure. If the neighbor is capable, the router sets OOBResync to true and forces the state machine to ExStart.

To keep routing stable, two rules change how the neighbor state is used. Moving to or from Full while the flag is set should not cause a new router-LSA or network-LSA to be originated. And explicit checks for Full for purposes other than LSDB synchronization and flooding should treat ExStart, Exchange and Loading as Full while the flag is set. Flooding and MaxAge-LSA procedures must keep looking only at the real state machine state.
sections.eli5: While the quiet resync is going on, the router keeps telling everyone else that the two routers are still working together, so nobody changes their routes.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
Because capable routers announce themselves with the LR-bit, no DBD packet with the R-bit set is sent to an incapable router. The LR-bit itself is transparent to OSPF implementations and does not affect communication between routers.

The Security Considerations section says only that the technique does not introduce any new security issues into OSPF. The IANA section refers to RFC 4813 for the Extended Options bit definitions.
sections.eli5: Routers that do not know the trick are never sent the special messages, so they are not confused.
